title: Modeling With Functions
bigQuestion: How do you turn a messy real question into math you can solve, and how do you know whether to trust the answer that comes back?

story.title: Emptying Soldier Field
story.kicker: A stadium on the lakefront, tens of thousands of people, and a question that has to be answered with a pencil before anyone opens a gate.
paragraphs: Soldier Field sits on Chicago's lakefront, just south of downtown, and it has held crowds since it opened in 1924. On a Bears Sunday more than sixty thousand people fill it. When the final whistle blows, all of them want to leave at once. Marcus, an engineering student on a class visit, is handed a question by the stadium's operations manager: "If we had to clear the seating bowl in ten minutes, could we?" There is no way to test it with a real crowd. He has to build a model.

Marcus starts with the simplest picture he can. Suppose 61,000 people are inside. Suppose the exits together can pass 100 people every second. Then the time to empty is 61,000 ÷ 100 = 610 seconds, a little over 10 minutes. He writes the model as a function: the number of people still inside after t seconds is N(t) = 61,000 − 100t, and the bowl is empty when N(t) = 0, at t = 610. Clean, quick, and probably wrong in a way he cannot yet see.

So he checks it against what he knows about crowds. At the final whistle, nobody is at the gates yet; people stand, gather their things and shuffle up the aisles. The exits do not run at full speed from second one. Marcus revises: the flow ramps up from 0 to 100 people per second over the first two minutes, then holds at 100. In those two minutes the average flow is 50 per second, so 50 × 120 = 6,000 people get out. The remaining 55,000 take 55,000 ÷ 100 = 550 seconds. Total: 120 + 550 = 670 seconds, about 11 minutes.

Then he asks the harder question: how sure is that 100 per second? If the true rate is 80, the main phase takes 55,000 ÷ 80 ≈ 688 seconds and the total is about 13.5 minutes. If it is 120, the total drops to about 9.6 minutes. So his honest answer is not one number but a range: roughly 10 to 13 minutes, depending mostly on the gate rate. That is the shape of every modeling problem in this chapter: a question, a set of assumptions, a function, a check against reality, a revision, and a result reported with its limits.
story.think: Which of Marcus's assumptions would you question first, and how could you test it without a stadium full of people?

lessons.title: From Question to Model
lessons.mainIdea: A model starts with a sharp question and a short list of assumptions, and the assumptions decide which math you can use.
reading: A school installs a water-bottle filling station. "Was it worth it?" is too vague to compute. A sharper question is: how many disposable bottles will students skip in one school year? To answer it you need *assumptions*, statements you accept as true for now so the math can begin. Suppose the school has 800 students, each uses the station 0.5 times per day instead of buying a bottle, and the year has 180 school days. Then bottles skipped = 800 × 0.5 × 180 = 72,000.

That calculation is a *model*: a simplified version of the situation written in math. Give its parts names, and it becomes a function you can reuse. Let S be the number of students, u the uses per student per day and D the school days; then B = S × u × D. Every assumption is a place the model could be wrong, so write them down in a list. Perhaps not every fill replaces a bottle; if only 1 in 4 does, the estimate drops to 72,000 ÷ 4 = 18,000. Perhaps attendance is not 100%.

The *modeling cycle* is the loop you walk around: ask a clear question, list assumptions, build the model, compute, check the result against reality, revise, and report. You rarely get it right the first time, and that is the point of the loop. A units check catches many errors early: students × (uses per student per day) × days = uses. If your formula ends in "students × days" with nothing per day, a factor is missing.

words.d: a simplified mathematical version of a real situation, built to answer a question
a statement you accept as true for now so that the math can begin
a quantity in a model that can take different values, named with a letter
the loop: question, assumptions, model, compute, check, revise, report

look.title: Pizza for the Club
look.text: A club with 120 members is ordering pizza. Assume every member comes, each eats 3 slices, and a pizza has 8 slices. Then slices needed = 120 × 3 = 360, and pizzas = 360 ÷ 8 = 45. As a model: P = (M × s)/8, where M is members and s is slices per member.
look.prompt: List two assumptions in this model that could be wrong. For each one, say how the number of pizzas would change if it were wrong.

check.q: A school has 600 students, each uses a filling station 0.4 times per day, and there are 180 school days. How many uses is that per year?
check.why: 600 × 0.4 = 240 uses per day, and 240 × 180 = 43,200 uses per year. Leaving out the 0.4 gives 108,000.

check.q: In the bottle model, which statement is an assumption rather than a measured fact?
choices: Every student comes to school every day
check.why: Enrollment, the calendar and bottle size can be looked up. Perfect attendance is a simplification chosen to make the math easier, so it must be listed as an assumption.

check.q: What is the first step of the modeling cycle?
choices: State a clear question with a measurable answer
check.why: Everything else depends on the question. Without knowing exactly what is being asked, you cannot choose assumptions or judge whether the answer is any good.

lessons.title: Checking and Revising
lessons.mainIdea: A model is checked against reality or common sense, and when it misses, you change an assumption and go around the cycle again.
reading: A cup of coffee starts at 90 °C in a 20 °C room. First model: it cools 10 degrees per minute, so T(t) = 90 − 10t. After 5 minutes it predicts 40 °C. After 10 minutes it predicts 90 − 100 = −10 °C. That is colder than the room, which cannot happen. The model has failed a *reality check*. The wrong assumption is "constant rate"; coffee cools fast when it is hot and slowly when it is nearly room temperature.

Revised model: the gap between coffee and room shrinks by the same percent each minute. The gap starts at 70 degrees. If it loses 10% a minute, T(t) = 20 + 70 × 0.9^t. At t = 10: 0.9^10 ≈ 0.349, so 70 × 0.349 ≈ 24.4, and T ≈ 44.4 °C. A thermometer reading of 45 °C at 10 minutes says the revised model is close. Notice that you did not fudge the answer; you changed an assumption and recomputed. That is what *revise* means.

Three checks catch most bad models. Check the *boundary cases*: at t = 0 the model gives 20 + 70 = 90, correct, and for very large t it approaches 20, the room, also correct. Check against a measured point, as we did at 10 minutes. Check the direction and size of change: cooling should slow down, and it does. A model that matches one data point can still be wrong, so use several checks, not one.

words.d: asking whether a model's output is even possible, like a temperature below the room's
change an assumption and rebuild the model, rather than adjusting the answer by hand
an extreme input, like time 0 or a very large time, where you know what the answer should be

look.title: Coffee Cooling, Measured
look.prompt: The linear model 90 − 10t predicts 40 at 5 minutes and −10 at 10 minutes. Which rows show it failing? Compute 20 + 70 × 0.9^t at t = 5 and t = 20 and compare.

check.q: What does the model T(t) = 20 + 70 × 0.9^t give at t = 0?
check.why: 0.9^0 = 1, so T(0) = 20 + 70 × 1 = 90 °C, the starting temperature. That is a boundary-case check the model passes.

check.q: A linear cooling model predicts −10 °C in a 20 °C room. What is the right response?
choices: Change the constant-rate assumption and rebuild the model
Replace the −10 with 20 and keep the model
Throw out the measurements that disagree
check.why: An impossible output means an assumption is wrong. Fix the assumption and recompute; do not patch the answer or ignore the data.

check.q: In the long run, what temperature does T(t) = 20 + 70 × 0.9^t approach?
check.why: As t grows, 0.9^t shrinks toward 0, so the 70 × 0.9^t part vanishes and T approaches 20 °C, the room temperature.

lessons.title: Reading Change in a Table
lessons.mainIdea: Constant first differences point to a linear model, constant second differences to a quadratic, and constant ratios to an exponential.
reading: A table with equally spaced inputs tells you its family if you look at how the outputs change. For x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 with y = 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, the *first differences* are 4, 4, 4, 4. Constant first differences mean a linear model, y = 4x + 3, with the difference as the slope. Check x = 4: 4(4) + 3 = 19.

For x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 with y = 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, the first differences are 3, 5, 7, 9. Not constant. Take the differences of those: 2, 2, 2. Constant *second differences* mean a quadratic, and the second difference equals 2a, so a = 1. Here y = x^2 + 1 fits every row: 1 + 1 = 2, 4 + 1 = 5, 9 + 1 = 10, 16 + 1 = 17, 25 + 1 = 26.

For x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 with y = 5, 10, 20, 40, 80, the first differences 5, 10, 20, 40 grow, but the ratios 10/5, 20/10, 40/20, 80/40 are all 2. A constant *ratio* means an exponential, y = 5 × 2^x. Real data are never this clean, so look for differences or ratios that are roughly constant. The common error is to see growing differences and shout "exponential" without checking ratios; a quadratic's differences also grow, but in a straight-line way.

One more caution: the inputs must be equally spaced for these tests to work. If x jumps 1, 2, 4, 8, the differences mean nothing, because each step covers a different distance. When a table has uneven spacing, either compute the change per unit of x or plot the points and look at the shape of the graph.

words.d: the amounts by which the outputs change from one row to the next
the differences of the first differences; constant for a quadratic
one output divided by the previous one; constant for an exponential
a group of functions with the same shape, like linear, quadratic or exponential

look.title: Which Family?
look.cite: a table built from a rule you are asked to find
look.prompt: Find the first differences and the ratios. Which family fits, and what is the rule? Test your rule on x = 4.

check.q: For x = 0, 1, 2, 3 a table gives y = 6, 11, 16, 21. Which model fits?
check.why: First differences are 5, 5, 5, so the model is linear with slope 5. At x = 0, y = 6, so the intercept is 6.

check.q: For x = 0, 1, 2, 3 a table gives y = 3, 6, 12, 24. Which family fits?
check.why: The ratios 6/3, 12/6 and 24/12 all equal 2, so y = 3 × 2^x. The first differences 3, 6, 12 are not constant.

check.q: A table's second differences are all 6. What is the coefficient a in the quadratic y = ax^2 + bx + c?
check.why: For a quadratic with unit spacing, the second difference equals 2a. So 2a = 6 and a = 3.

lessons.title: Clues in the Situation
lessons.mainIdea: Words in a situation signal a family: a fixed amount per unit means linear, a percent per unit means exponential, thrown objects and areas mean quadratic, and repeating cycles mean periodic.
reading: A taxi charges $3 plus $2.25 per mile. "Plus a fixed amount per mile" is the signature of a *linear* model: C(m) = 3 + 2.25m, so 10 miles cost 3 + 22.5 = $25.50. A bacteria culture doubles every 3 hours. "Doubles every" or "grows 5% each" is the signature of an *exponential*: N(t) = N_0 × 2^(t/3), so after 12 hours the count is 2^4 = 16 times the start.

A ball thrown upward at 40 feet per second from a height of 5 feet follows h(t) = −16t^2 + 40t + 5, in feet. Anything thrown, and any area that depends on a length, is *quadratic*. The ball peaks at t = 40/32 = 1.25 seconds, where h = −16(1.5625) + 50 + 5 = −25 + 55 = 30 feet. Hours of daylight in Chicago rise and fall every year, so daylight is *periodic* and calls for a sine or cosine. A rumor in a school of fixed size grows fast, then levels off as it runs out of people: that is *logistic*.

The trap is linear versus exponential when the word "percent" is nearby. "Grows by 5 a year" is linear; "grows by 5% a year" is exponential. Start both at 100 and run 20 years. Linear: 100 + 5 × 20 = 200. Exponential: 100 × 1.05^20 ≈ 100 × 2.653 ≈ 265. The gap only widens with time. When a situation mentions a rate, ask whether it is an amount per unit or a percent per unit before you choose.

words.d: changes by a fixed amount per unit of input; a constant slope
changes by a fixed percent or factor per unit of input
has an x^2 term; models thrown objects and areas
repeats the same pattern over and over, like daylight through a year
grows quickly at first, then levels off toward a ceiling

look.title: Five Situations
look.text: (1) A phone plan charges $20 plus $0.10 per text. (2) A savings account earns 4% per year. (3) The height of a stone dropped from a bridge. (4) The temperature in Chicago over a full day, hour by hour. (5) The number of students who have heard a rumor in a school of 900.
look.prompt: Match each situation to a family (linear, exponential, quadratic, periodic, logistic) and name the word or phrase that gave it away.

check.q: A culture of 500 bacteria doubles every 3 hours. How many are there after 12 hours?
check.why: 12 hours holds four 3-hour doublings, so the count is 500 × 2^4 = 500 × 16 = 8,000. Doubling only twice gives 2,000.

check.q: Which situation is best modeled by a quadratic function?
choices: A taxi fare that charges a fixed amount per mile
An account that earns 3% interest each year
The height of the tide through a week
The area of a square garden as its side length changes
check.why: Area is side × side, so A = s^2, a quadratic. The others are linear, exponential and periodic.

check.q: Which situation calls for a periodic model?
choices: Outdoor temperature over several days, repeating day and night
A savings account growing each year
A rock falling from a cliff
A phone plan with a fixed charge per text
check.why: Temperature repeats a similar rise and fall every 24 hours, so a periodic function fits. The others are exponential, quadratic and linear.

lessons.title: Fitting a Model to Data
lessons.mainIdea: Technology finds the line or curve of best fit, and residuals, actual minus predicted, tell you how well it fits and whether the family is right.
reading: Five students record hours studied and quiz scores: (1, 62), (2, 70), (3, 74), (4, 83), (5, 88). A calculator or spreadsheet computes the *line of best fit*, also called the *regression* line: y = 6.5x + 55.9. The slope says each extra hour goes with about 6.5 more points; the intercept, 55.9, is the model's score for zero hours. Predict 6 hours: 6.5(6) + 55.9 = 39 + 55.9 = 94.9.

How good is the fit? For each point, compute the *residual*: actual minus predicted. At x = 3 the line predicts 6.5(3) + 55.9 = 75.4, the actual score is 74, so the residual is 74 − 75.4 = −1.4. At x = 1: predicted 62.4, residual −0.4. At x = 4: predicted 81.9, residual 1.1. The residuals are small and scattered above and below zero, which is what a good fit looks like. If the residuals form a pattern, such as all negative in the middle and positive at the ends, the data are curving and you should try another family.

Technology also fits exponential and quadratic models, and reports the *correlation coefficient* r, which runs from −1 to 1. Values near 1 or −1 mean the points hug a line; values near 0 mean no linear pattern. Two cautions. First, a strong r does not prove that one thing causes the other. Second, do not *extrapolate* far beyond the data: 12 hours gives 6.5(12) + 55.9 = 133.9, more than 100 points, which is impossible. The model is only trusted where the data live.

words.d: the line that comes closest, overall, to a set of data points
the method technology uses to find the best-fitting line or curve
actual value minus the value the model predicts, for one data point
the number r between −1 and 1 that measures how tightly points follow a line
use a model outside the range of the data it was built from

look.title: Study Hours and Quiz Scores
look.cite: example class data; best-fit line y = 6.5x + 55.9
look.prompt: Use the line to predict each score, then find each residual. Are they small and mixed in sign? What does that say about the fit?

check.q: The line y = 6.5x + 55.9 predicts a score for 2 hours. The actual score was 70. What is the residual?
check.why: Predicted: 6.5(2) + 55.9 = 68.9. Residual = actual − predicted = 70 − 68.9 = 1.1. Subtracting the other way flips the sign.

check.q: A line's residuals are all negative in the middle of the data and positive at both ends. What should you do?
choices: Accept the fit, since some residuals are positive
Try a curved family, since the data bend
check.why: A pattern in the residuals means the line misses the shape of the data. Curved data call for a quadratic or exponential model.

check.q: The line y = 6.5x + 55.9 predicts 107.9 points for 8 hours of study. What does this show?
choices: A student who studies 8 hours will score 107.9
The slope of the line must be wrong
The model has a limit beyond the range of the data
check.why: A score above 100 is impossible, so the line cannot be trusted that far from the data (1 to 5 hours). That is the danger of extrapolating.

lessons.title: Combining Functions
lessons.mainIdea: Real models are often built from parts: subtracting cost from revenue, multiplying price by quantity, or feeding one function's output into another.
reading: A club sells T-shirts. Making them costs $200 for the design plus $4 per shirt, so C(x) = 200 + 4x. Each shirt sells for $12, so *revenue* is R(x) = 12x. *Profit* is what is left: P(x) = R(x) − C(x) = 12x − (200 + 4x) = 8x − 200. The *break-even* point is where profit is zero: 8x = 200, so x = 25 shirts. Check: 25 shirts bring in 12 × 25 = $300 and cost 200 + 100 = $300. Sell 40 and the profit is 8(40) − 200 = $120.

Sometimes one function feeds another. A store takes 20% off, so D(p) = 0.8p, and then the register adds 8% tax, so T(p) = 1.08p. Doing the discount first and then the tax is the *composition* T(D(p)) = 1.08 × 0.8p = 0.864p. Order does not matter for two multiplications. It matters when a $10 coupon is involved. Coupon then tax: 1.08(p − 10) = 1.08p − 10.8. Tax then coupon: 1.08p − 10. On a $50 item that is $43.20 versus $44.00.

Multiplying functions builds a model too. Suppose the number of shirts you can sell at price p is q(p) = 500 − 20p; raise the price and fewer people buy. Revenue is price times quantity: R(p) = p(500 − 20p) = 500p − 20p^2, a quadratic that opens downward. Its peak is at p = 500/40 = $12.50, where R = 500(12.5) − 20(156.25) = 6250 − 3125 = $3,125. Two linear pieces combined to make a quadratic with a best price, something neither piece showed alone.

words.d: the money taken in: price times number sold
revenue minus cost
the number sold at which profit is exactly zero
using the output of one function as the input of another, written f(g(x))

look.title: The Pizza Stand
look.text: A stand pays $350 to rent a booth and $5 in ingredients per pizza, so C(x) = 350 + 5x. Each pizza sells for $12, so R(x) = 12x. Profit: P(x) = 12x − (350 + 5x) = 7x − 350. Break-even: 7x = 350, so x = 50 pizzas.
look.prompt: Find the profit from 80 pizzas. Then explain what P(30) = −140 means for the stand.

check.q: Profit is P(x) = 8x − 200. What is the profit from selling 40 shirts?
check.why: P(40) = 8(40) − 200 = 320 − 200 = 120. Forgetting to subtract the $200 fixed cost gives 320.

check.q: Let f(x) = 0.8x and g(x) = x − 10. What is f(g(50))?
check.why: Work inside out: g(50) = 40, then f(40) = 0.8 × 40 = 32. Doing f first gives g(f(50)) = 40 − 10 = 30.

check.q: Revenue is R(p) = p(500 − 20p). What is the revenue at a price of $10?
check.why: At p = 10 the quantity is 500 − 200 = 300, and 10 × 300 = 3,000. Forgetting to multiply 20 by p gives 480 × 10 = 4,800.

lessons.title: Transforming a Model
lessons.mainIdea: Shifting, stretching or flipping a parent function adjusts a model to a new starting time, starting value or scale without changing its family.
reading: Chicago gets about 15 hours of daylight in late June and about 9 in late December, so the average is about 12 and the swing above or below it is about 3 hours. A sine wave with those numbers, with t the day of the year, is D(t) = 12 + 3 sin(2π(t − 80)/365). The 12 is a *vertical shift*: it lifts the wave from a middle of 0 to a middle of 12. The 3 is a vertical *stretch*: it makes the wave rise and fall 3 hours instead of 1. The (t − 80) is a *horizontal shift* that puts the upward crossing near day 80, around the spring equinox, and the 365 sets the period at one year.

The same moves adjust any *parent function*. A ball thrown from a 5-foot height follows h(t) = −16t^2 + 40t + 5. Throw it the same way from a balcony 20 feet higher and every height goes up 20: h(t) = −16t^2 + 40t + 25. Throw it 2 seconds later and the clock is shifted: h(t) = −16(t − 2)^2 + 40(t − 2) + 5. In general, f(x) + k moves a graph up k, f(x − h) moves it right h, a × f(x) stretches it vertically by a, and −f(x) flips it.

Horizontal shifts matter most with exponentials. A town of 1,200 people in 2010 grows 3% a year. The model P(t) = 1200 × 1.03^(t − 2010) uses the year directly; the shift makes the exponent count years since 2010. For 2025: 1200 × 1.03^15 ≈ 1200 × 1.558 ≈ 1,870. Forget the shift and you compute 1.03^2025, a number with 26 digits. Always ask what value of the input makes the exponent zero, and check that the model gives the starting value there.

words.d: the simplest function in a family, like sin(x), x^2 or 2^x
adding a constant to a function, which moves its graph up or down
replacing x with x − h, which moves the graph right by h
multiplying a function by a constant, which makes its rises and falls larger or smaller

look.title: Reading a Daylight Model
look.text: D(t) = 12 + 3 sin(2π(t − 80)/365) gives hours of daylight on day t of the year for a city like Chicago. On day 80 the sine is sin(0) = 0, so D = 12. About 91 days later, near day 171, the sine reaches 1, so D = 12 + 3 = 15. Near day 354 the sine is −1, so D = 9.
look.prompt: What would change in the formula for a city farther north, where daylight swings from 7 hours to 17 hours? Which number moves, and to what?

check.q: A ball follows h(t) = −16t^2 + 40t + 5. It is thrown the same way from a start 20 feet higher. Which model fits?
check.why: A higher start adds 20 to every height, which is a vertical shift: only the constant changes, from 5 to 25.

check.q: In D(t) = 12 + 3 sin(2π(t − 80)/365), what does the 3 represent?
choices: The hours the daylight swings above and below the average
The number of days in a cycle
The day of the year when daylight is longest
check.why: The 3 multiplies the sine, stretching its rise and fall from 1 to 3 hours. The 12 is the average, and 365 sets the period.

check.q: Why does the model P(t) = 1200 × 1.03^(t − 2010) subtract 2010 in the exponent?
choices: To slow the growth rate to 3%
So the exponent counts years since 2010 and P(2010) = 1200
Because the population was 2010 at the start
So the model works only before 2010
check.why: At t = 2010 the exponent is 0 and 1.03^0 = 1, so P = 1200, the starting value. The shift moves the clock's zero to 2010.

lessons.title: Piecewise Models
lessons.mainIdea: When the rule changes at a threshold, like a parking rate, a tax bracket or a shipping tier, a piecewise function models each piece on its own interval.
reading: A garage charges $5 for the first hour and $3 for each additional hour or any part of an hour. For 3.5 hours you pay $5 for hour one, then 2.5 extra hours round up to 3, so 5 + 3 × 3 = $14. A rule like this is a *piecewise function*: one formula on one *interval* of inputs, another formula on the next. Because the price jumps at each whole hour and stays flat in between, this piece is also a *step function*.

Income taxes use *thresholds* too. Take an example schedule: no tax on the first $10,000, 10% on the part from $10,000 to $40,000, and 20% on the part above $40,000. On $55,000 of income the tax is 0 + 0.10 × 30,000 + 0.20 × 15,000 = 3,000 + 3,000 = $6,000. The common error is charging 20% on all $55,000, which gives $11,000, nearly double. Written as a function: T(x) = 0 for x ≤ 10,000; T(x) = 0.10(x − 10,000) for 10,000 < x ≤ 40,000; T(x) = 3,000 + 0.20(x − 40,000) for x > 40,000. Check the seam at 40,000: the middle piece gives 0.10 × 30,000 = 3,000, and the top piece starts at 3,000, so the pieces meet.

The Soldier Field model from the chapter opening is piecewise as well. Let F(t) be the flow in people per minute at minute t. For 0 ≤ t ≤ 2 the flow ramps: F(t) = 3000t. For t > 2 it holds: F(t) = 6000. The number of people out by minute 2 is the average flow times the time, 3000 × 2 = 6,000, and after that 6,000 leave each minute, so by minute 10 the count is 6,000 + 8 × 6,000 = 54,000. A single formula could not capture the ramp and the plateau; two pieces do.

words.d: a function defined by different formulas on different intervals of the input
the input value where one rule stops and the next begins
a piecewise function whose value is constant on each interval and jumps at the thresholds
a stretch of input values, like 10,000 < x ≤ 40,000

look.title: Shipping Tiers
look.text: A shipping company charges $5 for a package up to 1 pound, $8 for over 1 pound up to 5 pounds, and $15 for over 5 pounds up to 20 pounds. The cost is a step function of weight w: 5 for w ≤ 1, 8 for 1 < w ≤ 5, 15 for 5 < w ≤ 20.
look.prompt: What does a 5.0-pound package cost? A 5.1-pound package? Why does it matter whether the threshold is written as ≤ 5 or < 5?

check.q: The garage charges $5 for the first hour and $3 per additional hour or part of an hour. What does 4.5 hours cost?
check.why: After the first hour, 3.5 extra hours round up to 4 hours: 5 + 3 × 4 = 17. Using 3.5 without rounding gives 15.50.

check.q: Using the example tax schedule (0% to $10,000, 10% from $10,000 to $40,000, 20% above), what is the tax on $30,000?
check.why: Only the part above $10,000 is taxed: 0.10 × (30,000 − 10,000) = 0.10 × 20,000 = 2,000. Taxing the whole $30,000 at 10% gives 3,000.

check.q: Which situation is best modeled by a step function?
choices: Parking that charges per hour or any part of an hour
Distance traveled at a steady speed
The area of a circle as its radius grows
check.why: The parking charge stays flat within each hour and jumps at each whole hour, the signature of a step function. The others change smoothly.

lessons.title: Error and Sensitivity
lessons.mainIdea: Every model's answer carries error from its inputs and assumptions, so test how much the answer moves when an input moves, and report a range rather than one number.
reading: In the Soldier Field model, 61,000 people at 100 per second gives 610 seconds. But the rate was a guess. Try 80 per second: 61,000 ÷ 80 = 762.5 seconds, about 12.7 minutes. Try 120: 61,000 ÷ 120 ≈ 508 seconds, about 8.5 minutes. Moving one input by 20% moved the answer by about 20% as well. That test is called *sensitivity* analysis, and it tells you which assumptions deserve the most care. An honest report gives the range: about 8.5 to 12.7 minutes.

When you can compare a model to a measurement, compute the *percent error*: |predicted − actual| ÷ actual × 100. The coffee model predicted 44.4 °C at 10 minutes and the thermometer read 45 °C, so the error is 0.6 ÷ 45 × 100 ≈ 1.3%. The *absolute error* is the plain difference, 0.6 degrees. Measurements carry their own error too: a length recorded as 12.5 cm to the nearest 0.1 cm could really be anywhere from 12.45 to 12.55 cm.

Errors spread through a calculation. A rectangle measured at 12.5 cm by 8.0 cm has an area of 100 cm^2 by the numbers. But the true sides could be as small as 12.45 and 7.95, giving 12.45 × 7.95 ≈ 98.98 cm^2, or as large as 12.55 and 8.05, giving 12.55 × 8.05 ≈ 101.03 cm^2. Reporting "100.0000" would claim a precision the measurements never had. Report the area as about 99 to 101 cm^2, an *interval estimate*.

words.d: how much a model's answer changes when one input changes
|predicted − actual| divided by actual, times 100
the plain difference between a predicted and an actual value, in the same units
a range of values, like 99 to 101 cm^2, instead of a single number

look.title: Time to Empty at Different Exit Rates
look.prompt: Which change makes the bigger difference: dropping the rate from 100 to 80, or raising it from 100 to 120? Why is the table not symmetric?

check.q: A model predicted 48 and the measured value was 50. What is the percent error?
check.why: |48 − 50| = 2, and 2 ÷ 50 × 100 = 4%. Dividing by the predicted 48 instead of the actual 50 gives about 4.2%.

check.q: If the exits pass only 50 people per second, how long does it take 61,000 people to leave?
check.why: 61,000 ÷ 50 = 1,220 seconds, and 1,220 ÷ 60 ≈ 20.3 minutes. Halving the rate doubles the time.

check.q: A model's answer barely changes when one input is changed by 20%. What does that tell you?
choices: The answer is not sensitive to that input
check.why: Low sensitivity means that input matters little to the result, so you can spend your effort checking the inputs that move the answer more.

lessons.title: The Limits of a Model
lessons.mainIdea: A model is only as good as its assumptions and its data range, so know where it stops applying and say so.
reading: An 8-year-old is 128 cm tall and has grown 6 cm a year. The linear model h = 128 + 6(a − 8) fits ages 6 to 10 well. Push it to age 30 and it predicts 128 + 6 × 22 = 260 cm, taller than any person who has ever lived. The model is not wrong; it was used outside its *domain of validity*, the range of inputs where its assumptions hold. Growth stops in the late teens, and the model never knew that.

Exponential growth has the same problem. In 1798 Thomas Malthus argued that populations tend to grow geometrically while food supplies grow arithmetically. In 1838 Pierre Verhulst proposed a fix, the *logistic model*, in which growth slows as the population nears a ceiling called the *carrying capacity*. One form is P(t) = 1000/(1 + 9 × 0.5^t), with t in days. At t = 0: 1000/(1 + 9) = 100. At t = 3: 0.5^3 = 0.125, so P = 1000/(1 + 1.125) = 1000/2.125 ≈ 471. At t = 10: 0.5^10 ≈ 0.00098, so P ≈ 1000/1.0088 ≈ 991. The curve starts like an exponential and flattens at 1000.

Other limits hide in plain sight. Models ignore randomness, so a real crowd will not empty on the same second twice. Inputs were measured once, under one set of conditions; a rainy day changes the gate rate. Assumptions can be unspoken: the Soldier Field model assumes everyone leaves at the final whistle and no gate is blocked. And precision can lie: reporting 10.1667 minutes when the rate is known only to ±20% pretends to a certainty you do not have. When a model guides a real decision, like how many gates to staff, it should be checked against a drill.

words.d: the range of inputs where a model's assumptions hold and its answers can be trusted
growth that starts like an exponential and levels off at a ceiling
the ceiling a logistic model approaches; the most the environment can support
using a model beyond the data or conditions it was built from

look.title: Logistic Growth in a Dish
look.prompt: An exponential model matched to days 0 and 2 would predict about 27,700 thousand on day 10. Which rows show the growth slowing, and what in the situation causes it?

check.q: What does P(t) = 1000/(1 + 9 × 0.5^t) give at t = 0?
check.why: 0.5^0 = 1, so the denominator is 1 + 9 = 10 and P = 1000/10 = 100.

check.q: A growth model built from ages 6 to 10 predicts a height of 260 cm at age 30. What went wrong?
choices: The model was used outside its domain of validity
The child's data were measured wrong
Linear models can never describe growth
check.why: The linear rule fit the ages it was built from. Growth stops in the late teens, so applying the rule at age 30 extrapolates past where its assumption holds.

check.q: In the long run, what does the logistic model P(t) = 1000/(1 + 9 × 0.5^t) approach?
check.why: As t grows, 0.5^t shrinks toward 0, so the denominator approaches 1 and P approaches 1000/1 = 1000.

lessons.title: Communicating a Result
lessons.mainIdea: A finished model is reported with the question, the assumptions, the method, the answer with its range, and what would change it.
reading: A model nobody can follow is not finished. A good report has five parts. The question: how long to empty Soldier Field? The assumptions: 61,000 people, a combined gate rate near 100 per second, a two-minute ramp-up. The method: a piecewise flow model, ramp then plateau. The answer with its range: about 11 minutes, likely between 9 and 13. The *limitations*: the rate is a guess, weather and blocked gates were ignored, and a drill should confirm it. A reader can now check every step and *reproduce* the number.

Show the model and the data together on one graph, with both axes labeled and units named. Mark the range where the model applies, and stop drawing it where it does not. In tables, round to a *precision* the inputs support: "about 10 minutes," not "10.1667 minutes." Then say what the number means for the decision. "Ten to thirteen minutes" matters only if the reader learns that the goal was ten, so the current gates are borderline.

The common failures are the same everywhere: hiding an assumption, reporting more digits than the data allow, leaving out the question so the number floats free, and choosing only the data that agree with you. A simple test is to hand your report to a classmate. If they can reproduce your answer from what you wrote, and can name the assumption they would attack first, the report is doing its job. That is the standard a transit planner, an engineer or a city budget analyst is held to as well.

words.d: a stated way the model could be wrong or a condition it does not cover
to get the same result again by following the report's stated steps
how many digits a number carries; it should match how well the inputs are known
the low and high values an answer could reasonably take

look.title: Two Reports
look.text: Report A: "It takes 10.1667 minutes to empty the stadium." Report B: "Assuming 61,000 people and about 100 people per second through all gates combined, the bowl empties in about 10 minutes. If the gate rate is 20% lower, it takes about 13 minutes. The rate should be checked with a drill."
look.prompt: Which report would help the operations manager decide whether to add gates, and why? Name two things Report A leaves out.

check.q: A model gives 10.1667 minutes, but its main input is known only to about ±20%. How should the answer be reported?
check.why: Extra digits claim precision the input does not have. Round to what the data support and give the range the input uncertainty produces.

check.q: Which of these must a model report include?
choices: The assumptions and where the model stops working
Only the final number, to keep it short
Every calculation but not the question
More digits than the data support
check.why: Readers can only judge and reproduce a result if they know the question, the assumptions and the model's limits.

check.q: What should a graph of a model and its data show?
choices: Only the model curve, extended in both directions
Labeled axes with units, the data and the model together, and the range where the model applies
Only the data points, with no axes labels
The model drawn far beyond the data to show trends
check.why: A reader needs to see how well the model fits the data and where it can be trusted, which requires labels, both data and model, and a marked range.

review.q: A model assumes 700 students each use a fountain 0.3 times a day for 180 days. How many uses per year?
review.why: 700 × 0.3 = 210 uses per day, and 210 × 180 = 37,800 per year.

review.q: For x = 0, 1, 2, 3 a table gives y = 2, 8, 32, 128. Which family fits?
review.why: The ratios 8/2, 32/8 and 128/32 all equal 4, so y = 2 × 4^x. The differences 6, 24, 96 are not constant.

review.q: Cost is C(x) = 150 + 6x and revenue is R(x) = 10x. At what number sold does the business break even?
review.why: Set 10x = 150 + 6x, so 4x = 150 and x = 37.5. The 38th item is the first that makes the profit positive.

review.q: A line of best fit predicts 85 for a data point whose actual value is 81. What is the residual?
review.why: Residual = actual − predicted = 81 − 85 = −4. The negative sign means the point lies below the line.

review.q: Using the chapter's example tax schedule (0% to $10,000, 10% from $10,000 to $40,000, 20% above), what is the tax on $50,000?
review.why: 0.10 × 30,000 = 3,000 on the middle bracket, plus 0.20 × 10,000 = 2,000 on the part above $40,000, totals $5,000.

review.q: A model predicts 200 and the measured value is 250. What is the percent error?
review.why: |200 − 250| = 50, and 50 ÷ 250 × 100 = 20%. Dividing by the predicted 200 instead gives 25%.

review.q: The model h(t) = −16t^2 + 30t + 4 describes a thrown ball. Which model describes the same throw from a start 10 feet higher?
review.why: A higher starting point adds 10 to every height, a vertical shift, so only the constant term changes from 4 to 14.

review.q: A logistic model P(t) = 500/(1 + 4 × 0.5^t) describes a population. What is its carrying capacity?
review.why: As t grows, 0.5^t vanishes and the denominator approaches 1, so P approaches 500. At t = 0 the population is 500/5 = 100.
